messages.content:
Rate the following clinical vignette:

He describes the day the ground first became his enemy. It was mid-morning, and he was at his desk in a high-rise office building in a city that rarely trembled. He remembers the low rumble that did not sound like thunder, the way his monitor began to wobble, and then the violent lurch that sent his chair rolling into the wall. The ceiling tiles fell like leaves. He crawled under his desk, hands over his head, and felt the building sway the way a tree bends in a gale. Each groan of concrete seemed to come from inside his own chest. The shaking lasted forty seconds. He still counts them every night in his head.

Now, at forty, he works from home as a software engineer, a job that once gave him a quiet sense of control. He can write code for hours, solving problems that follow predictable rules. But the control is an illusion. The moment his chair creaks, or a delivery truck rumbles past the window, his heart begins to gallop. He has stopped working in his second-floor home office. Instead, he sits on a floor cushion in the living room, his back pressed against the only interior wall. He tells his wife it helps his posture. He does not tell her that he maps every exit from the room and keeps the front door unlocked, even when they sleep.

His wife says he has become a ghost in his own life. He used to play chess with their son on Saturday mornings. Now he sits on the edge of the sofa, flinching at the slam of a cupboard door. He no longer rides the elevator in their apartment building. He takes the stairs, five flights, every time, and his knees ache by evening. At work, he turns down promotions that would require regular office meetings downtown. He tells his manager he prefers the quiet of home. But the quiet is not quiet. There is a constant hum of worry beneath his thoughts.

The nightmares began six months after the earthquake, and they have never left. In the dream, he is always at his desk, and the floor splits open like a mouth. He feels himself falling, and he wakes with his wife shaking his shoulder, asking who he is fighting. He does not tell her about the shame that follows-the image of his elderly neighbor who could not run, the sound of a child crying under a collapsed shelf. He reroutes his morning commute to avoid the street where the old hospital once stood. He cannot explain why. He simply cannot.

Concentration has become a luxury he no longer owns. A line of code that used to take minutes now takes an hour. He reads the same sentence three times, waiting for the meaning to arrive. His productivity has dropped, and he knows his team has noticed. He responds to messages with one-word answers. He avoids calls. When his phone buzzes, he startles as if it were an alarm.

He has not told his wife about the way his chest tightens in the grocery store, how he stands in the middle of the aisle and cannot remember what he came for. He has not told anyone that he keeps a go bag under the bed-a small duffel with bottled water, a flashlight, his son's stuffed rabbit. He checks it every Tuesday morning, as if the earth's plates are watching him. He knows this is not rational. But the feeling in his body is older than reason. He is still waiting for the shaking to stop.
